common_name: Hicaznar Pomegranate (BATEM Antalya Turkish Commercial Standard)

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root stock in late winter to early spring once hard freezes have passed; Hicaznar is the dominant Turkish commercial pomegranate, selected at the BATEM research station in Antalya for its balance of sweetness and acidity.

directions: Hicaznar accounts for the large majority of Turkey's pomegranate exports thanks to large, 300-450 gram fruit with a reliable 85 percent sweet to 15 percent tart aril balance that suits both fresh eating and juicing. Plant in full sun on well-drained ground and allow the soil to dry between deep waterings once established, since soggy roots invite crown and root rot in humid Gulf Coast summers. The fruit's exceptionally long storage life makes it useful for gardeners who want a single large harvest they can hold for months rather than a tree that trickles out fruit over many weeks. Thin dense interior growth each winter to keep air moving through the canopy, which helps limit the fungal leaf and fruit spots common in high-humidity climates.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Pomegranates for Texas
TUBITAK Turkish Journal of Agriculture and Forestry — Pomological Studies of Turkish Pomegranate Cultivars

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring on well-drained ground; Katirbasi is a traditional Sanliurfa-region Turkish pomegranate grown alongside Hicaznar and Suruc in southeastern Anatolia's old pomegranate districts.

directions: Katirbasi is one of the heritage pomegranate selections documented in Turkish pomological surveys of the Sanliurfa region, where growers blend its robust, assertive juice with the milder Hicaznar for traditional pomegranate molasses. In the home garden it behaves like other Mediterranean-climate pomegranates: it wants full sun, lean soil, and infrequent deep watering rather than rich, constantly moist ground. Expect a vigorous multi-trunk shrub that benefits from winter thinning to open the canopy, since Gulf Coast humidity makes good airflow more important for fruit and foliage health than it is in Katirbasi's native semi-arid range. Because it is a collector's variety rather than a nursery staple, gardeners may need to source budwood or cuttings through a rare-fruit exchange rather than a retail catalog.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
Turkish Journal of Agricultural and Natural Sciences — Agromorphological and Physico-Chemical Characterization of Sanliurfa Pomegranate Genetic Resources
California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Pomegranate Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring on well-drained ground; Surh-Anor ('red pomegranate' in Uzbek) buds out later than most pomegranates, which lets it dodge the late-winter frosts that damage earlier-blooming varieties.

directions: Surh-Anor is a Central Asian selection bred in a climate with cold winters and humid summer storms, and breeding trials in the Southeast have shown it holding up as well as the widely grown Salavatski in both productivity and resistance to arils rotting in wet weather. The pale yellow-pink skin and sweet, high-sugar, lightly speckled arils make it a good fresh-eating choice distinct from the deep-red commercial types already common in Gulf Coast gardens. Give it the same full sun and well-drained, lean soil every pomegranate wants, and resist the urge to overwater or over-fertilize, which pushes soft growth more prone to disease in muggy weather. Because its late budbreak also delays bloom, expect Surh-Anor to ripen slightly later in fall than early varieties like Russian types bred strictly for short seasons.
sources: Edible Landscaping — Surh-Anor Pomegranate
Pixies Gardens — Surh-Anor Pomegranate Tree
USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained ground; Suruc is a centuries-old pomegranate of the Sanliurfa region of southeastern Turkey that earned European Union protected-designation-of-origin status in 2023.

directions: Suruc is prized in its home region for a thin, elastic, yellowish rind and soft, easily removed arils with a sweet-sour balance that is eaten fresh rather than processed, unlike the more acidic Katirbasi it is often grown alongside. In Gulf Coast gardens treat it like any other Mediterranean pomegranate: full sun, well-drained and even poor soil, and deep but infrequent watering once the tree is established. Its thin skin is a double-edged trait in a humid climate, since it peels beautifully at the table but can also be more prone to splitting after heavy rain near harvest, so Gulf Coast growers should pick fruit promptly once it colors up rather than leaving it on the tree. As with other rare regional pomegranates, plan to source Suruc through a specialty or rare-fruit propagator rather than a mainstream retail nursery.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
European Commission eAmbrosia Geographical Indications Register — Suruc Nari PDO
California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Pomegranate Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant in late winter to early spring in full sun on well-drained ground; Dholka is one of India's oldest cultivated pomegranates, long grown around Gujarat for its large, juicy, soft-seeded fruit.

directions: Dholka bears large, 400 to 800 gram fruit with greenish-yellow rinds hiding soft, pinkish-white, juicy arils that lean more tart than the deep-red commercial pomegranates already common in American catalogs, giving Gulf Coast gardeners a genuinely different fresh-eating and juicing option. It was selected for drought tolerance in Gujarat's semi-arid climate, so in a wetter Gulf Coast garden the main adjustment is making sure drainage is excellent and irrigation is kept on the sparing side once roots are established. Like most pomegranates it flowers and fruits on new wood, so an annual light thinning in late winter keeps the shrub productive and lets light and air into the canopy, which matters more here than in its home climate because of higher disease pressure from humidity. Expect to track this variety down through a rare-fruit specialty grower rather than a mainstream nursery, since it is still uncommon outside Indian pomegranate-growing regions and collector circles in the US.
sources: USDA-ARS National Clonal Germplasm Repository, Davis, CA — Pomegranate Collection
ICAR-National Research Centre on Pomegranate — Cultivar Records
California Rare Fruit Growers Association — Pomegranate Fruit Facts

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed; Sunburst is a 1979 USDA Orlando release (Robinson x Osceola) that became Florida's most widely planted early-season tangerine.

directions: Sunburst produces medium, deep-orange, flattened fruit with thin, easily removed rind and rich, sweet juice, and it reliably sets a heavy crop when a compatible pollenizer mandarin is planted nearby, since it does not set well in solid single-variety plantings. The tree is thornless and naturally dense, so it makes an attractive dooryard specimen as well as a fruit producer, and it carries decent cold tolerance for the wood itself even though the thin-skinned fruit can still be marked by a hard freeze. Plant in full sun on well-drained soil, water deeply and regularly through fruit development, and protect young trees with frost cloth for their first few winters until the trunk calipers up. Because Sunburst needs cross-pollination to crop well, Gulf Coast gardeners should pair it with another mandarin or tangerine such as a satsuma already common in the area rather than relying on it alone.
sources: University of Florida IFAS EDIS — Sunburst Tangerine (CH079)
UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Sunburst Mandarin
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed; Nova is a 1942 USDA Orlando cross of Clementine mandarin and Orlando tangelo, a sibling of the Lee, Osceola, and Robinson mandarin hybrids.

directions: Nova colors and ripens notably earlier than its Orlando tangelo parent, giving Gulf Coast gardeners dark-orange, fine-textured, richly sweet fruit with a pebbled, easy-peeling rind well before most other mandarins are ready. It is counted among the more cold-tolerant tangerine hybrids bred at the old USDA Orlando station, a group that also includes Orlando, Lee, Robinson, and Osceola, making it a reasonable complement to satsuma in a Gulf Coast citrus planting. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil, water deeply and consistently while fruit is sizing, and plant a second, unrelated mandarin nearby since Nova sets better fruit with cross-pollination. Protect young wood through the first winters with frost cloth, as the tree's relative hardiness is still no substitute for real protection during an unusual hard freeze.
sources: UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Nova Mandarin
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Mandarin Hybrid Variety Notes
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed; Osceola is a 1942 USDA Orlando cross of Clementine mandarin and Orlando tangelo, released in 1959 and best known today as a parent of the more widely grown Sunburst tangerine.

directions: Osceola never became a major commercial crop because its small, highly colored fruit combines high sugar with equally high acid, but that same bold, tangy-sweet flavor makes it an interesting dooryard choice for gardeners who find standard mandarins one-note. The tree itself is upright, densely leafed, and nearly thornless, and it is counted among the more cold-tolerant of the old USDA Orlando mandarin hybrids even though its thin-skinned fruit still needs protection during hard freezes. Grow it in full sun on well-drained soil with regular deep watering through fruit set and sizing, and site it near a different mandarin or tangerine variety to improve pollination and fruit set. Because it was bred primarily as a breeding parent rather than a commercial fruit variety, expect to find it through specialty citrus nurseries rather than big-box garden centers.
sources: University of Florida IFAS EDIS — Osceola Citrus Hybrid (CH071)
UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Orlando Tangelo
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

common_name: Chandler Pummelo (Large Pink-Fleshed UC Riverside Pummelo)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has fully passed; Chandler was released in 1961 by UC Riverside breeders Cameron and Soost from a cross of Siamese Pink and Siamese Sweet pummelo.

directions: Chandler produces some of the largest citrus fruit a home gardener can grow, nearly round and up to four pounds, with thick yellow rind sometimes blushed pink and flesh that ranges from pale to deep pink depending on growing conditions. The flavor is sweet with only a mild grapefruit-like bitterness, and the texture is pleasantly juicy if a bit coarse, making it a worthwhile novelty alongside the satsumas and kumquats already common on the Gulf Coast. Give it a large growing space and expect a big, vigorous tree with somewhat pendulous branches, since pummelos are among the largest-growing citrus types. Because pummelos are more cold-sensitive than mandarins, site Chandler in the warmest, most sheltered spot available and be ready to cover or wrap young trees during freeze events, which are the main limiting factor for this variety in zone 9a.
sources: UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Chandler Pummelo
Four Winds Growers — Chandler Pummelo
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas

common_name: Cocktail Pummelo (Seedy Dooryard Pummelo-Mandarin Hybrid, Original UC Riverside Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has fully passed; Cocktail is a Siamese Sweet pummelo x Frua mandarin cross made at UC Riverside and later distributed informally through the nursery trade under its current name.

directions: Cocktail bears fruit anywhere from orange-sized to full grapefruit-sized, with thin yellow rind and juicy, orange-yellow flesh that carries a pleasant sub-acid flavor with floral and herbal notes rather than true grapefruit bitterness. It is too seedy to interest commercial growers, which is exactly why it remains a fun dooryard variety for gardeners who juice their own fruit and do not mind picking seeds out first. Plant in full sun with excellent drainage, water deeply through the growing season, and give it room, since it grows into a large, vigorous tree more in keeping with its pummelo parentage than its mandarin side. Protect it from hard freezes as you would any pummelo-type citrus, since the fruit holds well on the tree into early winter but the tree itself is more cold-sensitive than mandarins or satsumas already grown in zone 9a gardens.
sources: UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Cocktail Pummelo Hybrid
Greg Alder's Yard Posts — Cocktail Grapefruit Tree Profile
Four Winds Growers — Pummelo Hybrid Citrus

common_name: Palestine Sweet Lime (Low-Acid Middle Eastern Dooryard Lime)

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed; Palestine Sweet Lime is an old Middle Eastern selection valued for juice and fruit that is nearly acid-free rather than tart like a Key or Persian lime.

directions: Palestine Sweet Lime produces bright, greenish-yellow fruit with thin rind, few seeds, and very low-acid, mildly sweet juice, making it a gentler option for gardeners who want fresh lime flavor without sharp tartness, and its compact habit fits a smaller home-orchard footprint than many citrus. Plant in full sun in fast-draining soil, water deeply and consistently through fruit development, and avoid letting the root zone stay wet, since citrus of all kinds resent soggy feet in humid climates. It is more cold-sensitive than satsuma or kumquat and needs reliable protection below the low 30s, so in zone 9a it is best grown against a south-facing wall, in a large container that can be moved under cover, or in another frost-sheltered microclimate. Use the juice fresh in drinks or in Middle Eastern and Southeast Asian dishes that call for a milder, less acidic citrus note than standard limes provide.
sources: Four Winds Growers — Palestine Sweet Lime
US Citrus Nursery — Palestine Sweet Lime Tree
UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Palestine Sweet Lime

planting.note: Plant grafted trees in spring once frost danger has passed; Shekwasha is a small, flattened, intensely sour citrus native to Okinawa and Taiwan, grown there as a popular dooryard tree and juiced while still green.

directions: Shekwasha offers Gulf Coast gardeners something genuinely different from the sweet satsumas and kumquats already common in local plantings: small, flattened green-to-yellow fruit that is sharply sour even at full ripeness, prized in Okinawan cooking and drinks much the way a key lime or sour orange is used in the Gulf South. Its papeda heritage gives it somewhat better cold tolerance than many true mandarins, though it should still be treated as a protection-needed citrus rather than a satsuma-level survivor during hard freezes. Grow it in full sun on well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and water deeply and regularly since the species does not tolerate prolonged drought as well as some tougher citrus relatives. Use the juice and zest as a substitute for sour orange, yuzu, or lime wherever a bright, tart citrus note is wanted in marinades, dressings, or drinks.
sources: UC Riverside Citrus Variety Collection — Citrus depressa
Japan Food Research Laboratories — Shikuwasa (Citrus depressa) Characterization Studies
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Citrus for Texas
